items.text: We construct SCIVOCAB, a new WordPiece vocabulary on our scientiﬁc corpus using the SentencePiece1 library.
items.why: Explains the construction of the domain-specific vocabulary.
items.plain: We created SCIVOCAB, a new WordPiece token vocabulary built from our scientific papers using SentencePiece.

items.text: We produce both cased and uncased vocabularies and set the vocabulary size to 30K to match the size of BASEVOCAB.
items.why: Gives details on vocabulary casing and exact size.
items.plain: We made cased and uncased vocabularies set to 30,000 tokens to match BERT's default vocabulary size.

items.text: The resulting token overlap between BASEVOCAB and SCIVOCAB is 42%, illustrating a substantial difference in frequently used words between scientiﬁc and general domain texts.
items.why: Provides empirical evidence of domain shift in vocabulary overlap.
items.plain: The new scientific vocabulary overlaps by only 42% with the original BERT vocabulary, demonstrating major differences in common words.

items.text: Corpus We train SCIBERT on a random sample of 1.14M papers from Semantic Scholar (Ammar et al., 2018).
items.why: States the training dataset source and sample size.
items.plain: We trained SCIBERT on a random sample of 1.14 million scientific papers from Semantic Scholar.

items.text: This corpus consists of 18% papers from the computer science domain and 82% from the broad biomedical domain.
items.why: Describes the domain breakdown of the pretraining corpus.
items.plain: The pretraining corpus contains 18% computer science papers and 82% biomedical papers.

items.text: We use the full text of the papers, not just the abstracts.
items.why: Clarifies that full-text articles were used, not just abstracts.
items.plain: We trained the model on the full body text of the research papers rather than abstracts alone.

items.text: The average paper length is 154 sentences (2,769 tokens) resulting in a corpus size of 3.17B tokens, similar to the 3.3B tokens on which BERT was trained.
items.why: Reports key corpus size statistics in sentences and tokens.
items.plain: Papers averaged 154 sentences (2,769 tokens), totaling 3.17 billion tokens, which matches BERT's original 3.3 billion token size.

items.text: We train 4 different versions of SCIBERT: (i) cased or uncased and (ii) BASEVOCAB or SCIVOCAB.
items.why: Lists the four specific model variants produced for testing.
items.plain: We trained four versions of SCIBERT using either cased or uncased text and either the standard vocabulary or our scientific vocabulary.

items.text: The two models that use BASEVOCAB are ﬁnetuned from the corresponding BERT-Base models.
items.why: Explains how variants using the original vocabulary were initialized.
items.plain: The two models that kept the original BERT vocabulary were fine-tuned directly from the existing pretrained BERT-Base models.

items.text: The other two models that use the new SCIVOCAB are trained from scratch.
items.why: Explains initialization for variants using the scientific vocabulary.
items.plain: The two models using the new scientific vocabulary were pretrained entirely from scratch.

items.text: Following the original BERT code, we set a maximum sentence length of 128 tokens, and train the model until the training loss stops decreasing.
items.why: Details the multi-stage training sequence and length limit.
items.plain: We initially limited inputs to 128 tokens per sentence and trained until the training loss plateaued.

items.text: We then continue training the model allowing sentence lengths up to 512 tokens.
items.why: Describes the second pretraining phase with longer context lengths.
items.plain: After the first training stage, we continued pretraining while allowing sentence lengths up to 512 tokens.

items.text: CLS and REL), we feed the ﬁnal BERT vector for the [CLS] token into a linear classiﬁcation layer.
items.why: Describes the specific model architecture for sentence classification tasks.
items.plain: For sequence and relation classification, we pass the output vector of the special classification token into a linear classifier.

items.text: NER and PICO), we feed the ﬁnal BERT vector for each token into a linear classiﬁcation layer with softmax output.
items.why: Describes the model architecture used for sequence labeling tasks.
items.plain: For named entity recognition and trial span extraction, each token's output vector goes to a linear layer with a softmax activation.

items.text: We differ slightly in using an additional conditional random ﬁeld, which made evaluation easier by guaranteeing well-formed entities.
items.why: Notes a structural departure from standard BERT using a CRF layer.
items.plain: Unlike standard BERT setups, we added a conditional random field layer to ensure output entity labels were formatted correctly.

items.text: For DEP, we use the model from Dozat and Manning (2017) with dependency tag and arc embeddings of size 100 and biafﬁne matrix attention over BERT vectors instead of stacked BiLSTMs.
items.why: Details the architecture adaptions for dependency parsing.
items.plain: For parsing, we replaced stacked BiLSTMs with biaffine matrix attention over BERT vectors alongside tag and arc embeddings of size 100.

items.text: We ﬁnetune for 2 to 5 epochs using a batch size of 32 and a learning rate of 5e-6, 1e-5, 2e-5, or 5e-5 with a slanted triangular schedule (Howard and Ruder, 2018) which is equivalent to the linear warmup followed by linear decay (Devlin et al., 2019).
items.why: Gives fine-tuning hyperparameter details including learning rates and schedule.
items.plain: We fine-tuned models for 2 to 5 epochs with batch size 32, learning rates from 5e-6 to 5e-5, and a slanted triangular schedule.

items.text: We also explore the usage of BERT as pretrained contextualized word embeddings, like ELMo (Peters et al., 2018), by training simple task-speciﬁc models atop frozen BERT embeddings.
items.why: Explains the frozen-embedding baseline architecture setup.
items.plain: We evaluated frozen BERT vectors as static contextual embeddings by training simple task-specific neural networks on top of them.

items.text: For text classiﬁcation, we feed each sentence of BERT vectors into a 2-layer BiLSTM of size 200 and apply a multilayer perceptron (with hidden size 200) on the concatenated ﬁrst and last BiLSTM vectors.
items.why: Describes task head architecture used over frozen embeddings for classification.
items.plain: For classification with frozen embeddings, sentence vectors go through a two-layer BiLSTM of size 200 followed by a multilayer perceptron.

items.text: We optimize cross entropy loss using Adam, but holding BERT weights frozen and applying a dropout of 0.5.
items.why: States optimization parameters for frozen embedding models.
items.plain: When BERT weights were kept frozen, we trained the task layers using Adam, a dropout rate of 0.5, and cross-entropy loss.

items.text: We observe that SCIBERT outperforms BERT-Base on scientiﬁc tasks (+2.11 F1 with ﬁnetuning and +2.43 F1 without)8.
items.why: Provides overall metric comparison between SCIBERT and BERT-Base.
items.plain: SCIBERT outperformed BERT-Base on scientific tasks by 2.11 F1 points with fine-tuning and 2.43 F1 points with frozen embeddings.

items.text: We observe that SCIBERT outperforms BERT- Base on biomedical tasks (+1.92 F1 with ﬁnetuning and +3.59 F1 without).
items.why: Reports specific performance gains on biomedical NLP benchmarks.
items.plain: SCIBERT outperformed BERT-Base on biomedical datasets by 1.92 F1 with fine-tuning and 3.59 F1 with frozen embeddings.

items.text: We observe that SCIBERT outperforms BERT- Base on computer science tasks (+3.55 F1 with ﬁnetuning and +1.13 F1 without).
items.why: Reports specific performance gains on computer science benchmarks.
items.plain: SCIBERT outperformed BERT-Base on computer science datasets by 3.55 F1 with fine-tuning and 1.13 F1 without.

items.text: We observe improved results via BERT ﬁnetuning rather than task-speciﬁc architectures atop frozen embeddings (+3.25 F1 with SCIBERT and +3.58 with BERT-Base, on average).
items.why: Compares full fine-tuning directly against frozen embedding representations.
items.plain: Fine-tuning the whole model beat using frozen embeddings by an average of 3.25 F1 for SCIBERT and 3.58 F1 for BERT-Base.

items.text: Averaged across datasets, we observe +0.60 F1 when using SCIVOCAB.
items.why: Quantifies the exact performance contribution of the custom scientific vocabulary.
items.plain: Switching from the standard vocabulary to the new scientific vocabulary yielded an average improvement of 0.60 F1.

items.text: Given the disjoint vocabularies (Section 2) and the magnitude of improvement over BERT-Base (Section 4), we suspect that while an in-domain vocabulary is helpful, SCIBERT beneﬁts most from the scientiﬁc corpus pretraining.
items.why: Draws key conclusion on corpus pretraining vs. vocabulary contribution.
items.plain: Although an in-domain vocabulary helps, pretraining on the scientific text corpus accounts for most of SCIBERT's performance gains.
